extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary_biologists, and educated general readers interested in sexual selection
extracted.subtask_description: Use observational, comparative, and behavioral evidence to evaluate whether particular traits (colours, sounds, ornaments, behaviours) in animals have arisen by sexual selection rather than by natural selection or other causes. Focuses on sex-differences, courtship, parental care, and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female choice implied by male courtship and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: “The males sedulously court the females... Can it be believed that they would thus act to no purpose during their courtship? And this would be the case, unless the females exert some choice and select those males which please or excite them most.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of males actively courting, displaying bright colours, or otherwise showing ornamentation in the presence of females are taken as evidence that females exercise choice; if females select mates, male ornamentation is intelligible as a product of sexual selection. Example: stickleback males display brilliant throat and belly colours during breeding-season and perform courtship behaviours; thus female choice is inferred. Consider whether courtship acts plausibly function to attract or stimulate females rather than serving only other purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal development and display of male ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: “In other species the males become brighter than the females and otherwise more highly ornamented, only during the season of love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits that appear or intensify specifically during the breeding season (e.g., bright breeding colours, crests, throat pouches) support sexual selection as their function is tied to mating. Note ontogenetic timing: juveniles and non-breeding adults resembling females while breeding males differ strongly argues for sexual rather than purely protective function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male courtship behaviours that actively solicit females
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: males excavate hollows as nests and ‘endeavours in the most persuasive manner to induce a female... to share it’; males expand fins, bound about females, blow air/mucus to form froth-discs and collect fertilised ova, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active behaviours that appear to display or to invite mating (nest offering, fin-presentation, vivid movement near females) are criteria for sexual selection. Record detailed behavioural sequences and whether females respond preferentially. Distinguish display behaviours from purely functional acts (e.g., nest construction that serves only protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Male–male competition (fighting) for females
rubrics_metrics.description: “The males fight for the possession of the females.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of males fighting, mounting vigilant guard over nests, or driving away rival males indicate sexual selection via male–male rivalry. Examples include Labrus males guarding hollows, lizards and anoles battling, and males defending nests. Presence of combat and subsequent reproductive monopolization strengthen inference of sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-specific or sex-limited structures (sex-limited inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “With most fishes, in which the sexes differ in colour or in other ornamental characters, the males originally varied, with their variations transmitted to the same sex, and accumulated through sexual selection...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits found primarily or exclusively in one sex (e.g., sound-producing bones in males, marsupial-like brood pouches in male pipe-fish, male throat pouches) are evidence that selection acted differently on sexes; consider patterns of inheritance and whether traits are transmitted primarily to the sex exhibiting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of male traits to females by ordinary transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: “In many cases, however, such characters have been transferred, either partially or completely, to the females.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When both sexes are similarly ornamented, this can be explained by ancestral male traits being inherited equally by females rather than by selection acting on females. Evaluate phylogenetic and breeding-season patterns to determine whether similarity results from transfer from males or from selection on both sexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental care patterns and their implications for selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin notes many species where males take exclusive charge of nests and young, yet males are often the more conspicuously coloured; he argues that in such cases the death of a male during incubation would more strongly affect the offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine which sex provides parental care and how that affects selection on conspicuous traits: if the caring sex is highly conspicuous, protective coloration is less likely to explain the ornament; persistent bright male traits despite male parental importance support sexual selection. Also consider whether care leads to sex-role reversal (see Solenostoma example where female is brighter and hatches eggs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanation — protective/camouflaging coloration
rubrics_metrics.description: “With some fishes, as with many of the lowest animals, splendid colours may be the direct result of the nature of their tissues and of the surrounding conditions... certain fishes... may have been rendered conspicuous in order to warn birds and beasts of prey that they were unpalatable... many fishes... are brightly coloured in order to escape detection by their enemies [Wallace’s view].”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always test sexual-selection hypotheses against the possibility that colours/marks function for concealment, warning (aposematism), mimicry, or environmental matching. Use habitat data (e.g., presence/absence of colourful coral), predator interactions, and field experiments to rule in/out protective functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanation — artificial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The gold-fish... is perhaps a case in point, as it may owe its splendid colours to a single abrupt variation... It is, however, more probable that these colours have been intensified through artificial selection...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where species have long histories of human breeding, consider artificial selection as a plausible cause of extreme ornamentation. Historical records and domestication context are relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of male-specific acoustic or sound-producing organs and vocalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most interesting case for us is that of two species of Ophidium, in which the males alone are provided with a sound-producing apparatus... From this statement... it is almost certain that... sound-producing instruments have... been developed through sexual selection, as a means for bringing the sexes together.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Male-limited acoustical structures and breeding-season vocalizations (drumming, flute-like notes) suggest sexual selection if they function to attract mates or coordinate mating. Document anatomical specialization correlated with sound production and its timing with reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogenetic pattern: young and non-breeding forms resemble females
rubrics_metrics.description: “In many species the males whilst young resemble the females in colour; but when adult become much more brilliant, and retain their colours throughout life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When juveniles of both sexes resemble adult females and bright ornamentation appears only in mature males, this supports sexual selection. Record developmental trajectory of traits across ages and sexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/ecological correlation must fit hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin critiques Wallace’s idea that reef fishes are brightly coloured for crypsis by pointing out bright species in Amazon fresh-waters where corals are absent and asking whether habitat correlations truly support protective explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test putative functions by comparing species across habitats: if bright colours appear where protective mimicry is impossible (e.g., no colourful substrate), sexual selection is more plausible. Use broad comparative data to evaluate competing hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry/convergence as non-sexual causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin cites the coral-snake example: harmless species resembling venomous ones likely acquired colours as protection by imitation; thus mimicry can explain some conspicuous colouration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether similar colour patterns across sympatric species reflect Batesian/Müllerian mimicry instead of sexual selection. Look for co-occurrence of model and mimic species, predator avoidance evidence, and phylogenetic independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-reversal or female-brightness as evidence for different selective regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The exceptional case of Solenostoma: “the female is much more vividly-coloured and spotted than the male, and she alone has a marsupial sack and hatches the eggs... the female of Solenostoma differs from all the other Lophobranchii... in being more brightly-coloured than the male.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases where the typical sexual roles are reversed (female more ornamented and performing care/hatching) point to reversed sexual selection or male choice. Record which sex courts, which provides care, and which is ornamented to interpret selective pressures correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral and morphological complexity as convergent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin uses multiple independent lines (colours, courtship acts, nest-building, sound production, seasonal timing, sex-limited anatomy) together to argue for sexual selection in many groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong inference of sexual selection arises when several independent indicators co-occur: male-limited ornaments, active courtship, male–male competition, breeding-season timing, and female responsiveness. Assemble multidisciplinary evidence (anatomy, behaviour, ecology) before concluding sexual selection is responsible.
